blocks.x: Willie Josephs You say Willie Josephs then was your brother. Is he a younger brother?

No, I have a younger brother who played music too in the country. Henry Josephs used to play with Phil Bonne William. Oh, yes. He played with Freddie Landry. I played with Freddie Landry. Freddie Landry played with Freddie Landry. After he got his own band.
And then your brother who died, what was his name? Willie Josephs. The other one?
Willie the other one, I'd better call him Kaiser. Yeah.
Why was he called Kaiser? I never did know.
Kaiser. And the one here, the barbush was Nelson Josephs.
And what did he play? Laramie. Oh, see.
1916. Actually, the other game was the first band I played with. Oh, yeah. The first band I played was a little band with women girls. Oh, is that right? In the country.
Oh.
Yeah, the band here. Talk about the Prince Bank too. Have you heard about him? Oh, yes. You heard about him? Yes. The first band I played in the yard when I first came in.
I never knew him, but...
I know... He was the man. You heard of him? I knew him. I knew him. I've been to his home.
Yeah.
Heard him play.
Lawrence Dewey. Yes, I know him. Out in Lafayette. Yeah. Well, you and Bro went out to see him, did you?
Yes, we went out there almost a year and a half ago. Uh-huh. Now, where were you born?
I was born in St. James. About 11 miles on this side of Donisonville.
Was that in a town or was it...
In a little village in Southerment. Yeah.
What's the name of it?
Jamestown.
Jamestown.
Jamestown. Jamestown. Jamestown is 11 miles from Donisonville. Oh, yeah.
I've been here 19... 19...
19... 19... 6... Since 19 and 6 you've been born. What was the date you were born? Your birthday. Well, uh... I met...
80... 27 November. I just remember the days of...
27 November. 27 November. You'll find out. 27 November.
You'll find out. Yeah. I'll find out. I'll find out. I'll find out. I'll find out. I'll find out. I'll find out. I'll find out. I'll find out.
27 November. Of November. You'll make 80.
You mean tomorrow?
Yes, that's it. Tomorrow is your birthday? Uh-huh. Well, I'll be. Yeah.
Really?
I'll make 80 tomorrow.
Did your father play music or something?
Yeah.
Father and my uncle play it.
Well, by the way, if you'd like to sit down any time, we can move another chair around. That'd be okay, yeah.
Would you rather sit down someplace?
Yeah, that's right. I'd be more comfortable.
I think so, too.
Might as well rest. We'll move this over here. I think these chairs. Over here. Keeps that?
Yeah. You take a look. I'll get a stronger cap on me. That's good enough.
That'll pick up, I think, pretty easily there. You don't have to talk loud or anything. Just talk to your natural tone of voice. You can see.
It'll pick everything up in the holder. Yeah. Yeah.

All right. That'll get a stronger cap on me. That'll get a stronger cap on me. Yeah. That'll get a stronger cap on me. Yeah. That'll get a stronger cap on me. That'll get a stronger cap on me. Yeah. That'll get a stronger cap on me. Yeah. That'll get a stronger cap on me. That'll get a stronger cap on me. That'll get a stronger cap on me.
That'll get a stronger cap on me.
That'll get a stronger cap on me. When did you start to play music up in the country?
In the country I was about eleven years old. A little band with my uncle in the country.
What instrument did you play first?
First instrument was bass. You started on the bass when I was a kid. The bass, violin, man, yuk, all the kind of instruments.
Did you make your own bass or was it a big bass?
It was a bass I bought, three string bass, years ago.
What was your uncle's name by the way?
I bought Philo-Jean Joseph.
Philo-Jean?

Yeah, he was French, you know. My dad was Val-Saint Joseph, a French name. And Gustave Joseph, the youngest uncle. Did he play? Me, Joseph. They all played with some. All of them did play some. Five brothers of us, all of us played music. And Kaiser, he played many different bands here, and myself.
Were you the oldest of the brothers?
The oldest brothers, yeah. The oldest?
Yeah.
What was Kaiser's age? Was he younger? How much younger?
Well, his age when he died, I believe he was about 70. About 70 years old. 70? Yeah.
He was the one that had the accident, was run over, hit by the car.

Right. Phillip and Howard. He was coming here to the shop, yeah. And he had been away about, I'll say about eight years. And he hadn't been here a month before. Somebody told me he'd been in California, is that right? That's why he was in California.
But over there, they take care, they don't, they see somebody walking, they have to stop, you know. That's right.
But here they don't do it. He was just going on the sidewalk. The first foot on the sidewalk, I had to pick them up.
Right.
Hit and run.
Yeah, hit and run, never lose. Yeah, that's right.
A car that you wouldn't give, three dollars for, you see?
That's an old, raggedy car. So when did he start on the clarinet? Was he playing up in the country too, I guess?
He started on a C clarinet. A C? I was down here and I bought a C clarinet and he was playing by air.
He learned down here in New Orleans?
No, he learned in the country. Up in the country?
Up in the country, yeah. But you got the clarinet down here?
Yeah, got the center tuned. And he later on, he played saxophone, that's why he started reading. And it was pretty good. He played with every band in the city pretty much, you know. Yeah.
I know he made those records with Louis Dumaine.
Louis Dumaine, that's right. I used to play with it myself.
You played with Louis Dumaine?
Louis Dumaine, there's three of them. Me and my brother here, Nelson Joseph, Kaiser. And the first Kaiser by the name of Louis Joseph. Always Louis Dumaine's band.
Well, it was Kaiser's, was that his second name or how did they call it?
Well, his first name is Willie, his right name is Willie Joseph. Willie Joseph, yes.
Where'd you get that name of Kaiser?
How'd they? Oh, I don't know. During the war, World War I. World War I, they called him Kaiser, you know.
Wow.
Yeah. Sure.
Because some people just call him Willie Kaiser, they don't even call him Willie Joseph.
No, that's right, Willie Kaiser.
I thought that was his last name one time.
Yeah. Mm-hmm. Oh, you want to know something about Holmes? Oh, yes.
Get the picture.
Oh, you got that picture of him.
Mm-hmm. That's the picture of the, uh, Professor Holmes. It's a really, it's a regular brass band, I guess.
A regular brass band.
It says the Holmes band of Lutcher, Louisiana.
It's a whole band of Lutcher, Louisiana. This is Anthony Holmes, that's his name.
The cornet player on the right.
On the right. On the right. Dennis Harris, maybe you might have heard of him.
No.
Is this trombonist?
No, clarinet.
Oh, I couldn't see. Clarinet. He's a bass drum player. Mm-hmm.
Baritone. Baritone.

Now this guy here, we used to call him Nug. He's got one hand, that's all I've been known. That's the only name. And he was a bass drum player. Bass drum player. John Porter's brother, he's Joe Porter. Cornet. Second, second cornet. Floyd Jackson, bass player. David Jones, I know you heard of him.
Oh yes, he's out in California.
He was playing snare drum. He didn't like that. I didn't know he was a snare drum player.
That's new to me.
He said he played all instruments. All instruments, that's what he do now. He plays all instruments.
Now the trombone player, you're saying he played slide, huh?
Slide, that's one of the first slides I've ever seen. I've been here for years. He brought a slide here when he didn't have any here in yours. Henry Sawyer.
Henry Sawyer. That's right. See, how many players are there? One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight pieces.
They came down here in those time and outplayed all of the band down here. Brass band, you know? Short band.
Did they use any alto horns ever in that group? I think they have two cardinals clarinets.
Well, they don't have no alto.
Baritone, one trombone. He took alto.

David Jones. David Jones, he took alto. Melo phone, you know? Yes. Later on he picked up saxophone. Now I had the first saxophone in New Orleans. You had the first saxophone? First saxophone. I put on the bass saxophone. I had saxophone in 1914. They used to travel. They used to travel. They used to travel. They used to travel to shows.
Different shows.
Like carnival or circuses? Circus, yeah. Circus? Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. What year would that be that that picture was taken about? Do you know any of these? I see. Before World War I or after?
Oh yes, a long time before World War I. That's before I knew them people. Mm-hmm . About five or six years before.
Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Before World War I or after?
Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
About five or six years before World War I.
Yeah.
Let's see that's before the storm.
Yeah. He was the youngest one in the band, Laurie Jackson.
He tuba played?
Tuba played, played piano. Played trumpet, played piano.
Was he related to any of the other Jacksons?
No.
I just wondered about Eddie Jackson.
No. If he can't. He was born in Lodzha. In Bridge City now, that's where he is now. No play anymore.
He's still up there in Bridge City then. We'll have to talk to him someday.
Still there, yeah. Well, there's about only two men living. There's two, let's see. There's three men living on that picture.
Which one's your name? David Jones.
David Jones, Floyd Jackson, Henry Sawyer.
Oh, the trombonist, he's still, where is he?
No, he's not playing. He's your son. Can't hardly see. Mm-hmm. You would like to talk to him?
Yes. Oh, yes we would. He's over in the, uh, Al Jarrell.
No, he's here. He live in here.
Oh, he lives.
He's here. The trombonist. I can find out from his nephew, you know, his nephew. Oh, we certainly would appreciate that. I can find out and I'll let you know. Oh.
We would like to talk to him. Oh, he lived.

That's his nephew for the afternoon. And you think he was the first one that brought the slide then? I believe he was the first man that I know that had a slide, brought a slide here from Lutcher in Yard.
Oh, where did you get your saxophone? My saxophone?

Well, I was playing bass with the same band, Professor Holmes. And he said, John, you have a man like you shouldn't be on the bass. I got a shell, see? And I got the shell, played the shell a while, and said, why don't you get your saxophone? I'll get you saxophone pretty cheap. So, a friend of mine was there at the time, they said, I know a fella in Yardin. Just came from New York with a saxophone. I just bought it. So, I gave him, they said he wanted fifty dollars for it, and I gave him fifty dollars to train pad, that he played alto saxophone. And that's the one he wanted me to play, he played alto.
And you played it with the Holmes band?
I played with the Holmes band. Well, I could play the clarinet, I could play clarinet. And about a month, I was going out with the band, with the saxophone.
So, you took up clarinet first?
First, yeah. E flat clarinet, I used to play in the brass band, I used to play for them a while.
Well, we never did get your first job straight, that was your uncle? Who's that? And on your very first job, you said that was in the country with your uncle and bro?
My uncle, my two uncle, and bro, and my brother. They were one, Nelson Joseph, you know, the one at the shop, yes.
And what instruments were they playing then?
Well, uh, clarinet. That was who?
Violin.
I was playing bass, and one of my brothers was playing guitar, Nelson Joseph.
And what was bro playing?
Bro was playing mandolin, yeah.
And your two uncles played clarinet and violin?
Oh, one played, one played, uh, one of my uncles playing violin, two violin. Oh, two violin. And one played guitar. Oh, my brother, my brother. My brother.

A fellow by the name of Joe, you were saying? A fellow by the name of Joe Poche, and he was some professor in them days, and I was young myself. You know what I managed to do? A man like that was cutting cane. You know about cutting cane. He would hear and guide. He would hear and guide.
Now you work with John Kazimer?
I work with Kazimer in orchestra. In the orchestra? In the orchestra, not in the brass band. I work in the brass band.
Did you work with him when Wooden Joe used to be with him? Wooden Joe Nicholas? Wooden Joe, you remember Joe? Yes, I made some records with him.
He used to play right over here in Los Angeles.

segments.title: Brothers Henry, Willie 'Kaiser' and Nelson Joseph
segments.summary: Joseph names his younger brother Henry, who played with Freddie Landry, and his brothers Willie (called Kaiser) and Nelson.

segments.title: First band with country girls; Prince Bank and Lawrence Duhé
segments.summary: His first band was a little country group of girls; he recalls hearing and visiting an admired bandleader and Lawrence Duhé in Lafayette.

segments.title: Birthplace Jamestown, his birthday, and a musical father and uncle
segments.summary: He was born in Jamestown near Donaldsonville; his birthday is the next day, when he turns 80. His father and uncle played music.

segments.title: Getting settled for the recording
segments.summary: Chairs and the microphone are arranged for comfort.

segments.title: Starting on bass at eleven in the family band
segments.summary: He started at about eleven with an uncle's country band on a three-string bass; five Joseph brothers all played music.

segments.title: Kaiser's death in a hit-and-run
segments.summary: Kaiser, about 70, was killed by a car after returning from California.

segments.title: Kaiser's clarinet, saxophone, Louis Dumaine and the nickname
segments.summary: Kaiser learned clarinet by ear in the country, later played saxophone and with every band, including Louis Dumaine's, and was nicknamed Kaiser in World War I.

segments.title: Identifying the Professor Holmes band photo from Lutcher
segments.summary: Looking at a photo of the Holmes brass band of Lutcher, Joseph names the members and instruments.

segments.title: Having the first saxophone in New Orleans; dating the photo
segments.summary: He claims the first saxophone in New Orleans in 1914; the photo is dated five or six years before World War I.

segments.title: Surviving Holmes band members and the first slide trombone
segments.summary: He describes Laurie Jackson and the three men still living, and the trombonist who brought a slide from Lutcher.

segments.title: Buying his saxophone while playing bass with Holmes
segments.summary: With Holmes's encouragement he bought an alto saxophone for fifty dollars and was soon playing it with the band; clarinet came first.

segments.title: His first job with uncles and brothers
segments.summary: His first job was in the country with two uncles and his brothers on bass, guitar, mandolin and violins.

segments.title: Joe Poche, a professor in the country
segments.summary: A fragment about a cane cutter named Joe Poche who was a 'professor'.

segments.title: Working with John Casimir and Wooden Joe
segments.summary: He worked in Casimir's orchestra, and mentions recording with Wooden Joe.
